Neonates of the Southern banded newt measure approximately 1 centimeter [Lb = approximately 1 centimeter] at birth, a diminutive size that reflects the substantial yolk reserves allocated to each fertilised ovum within the gelatinous egg mass. This length at birth is comparable to that observed in the congeneric Neurergus kaiseri, whose larvae emerge at a similar stage of development after the chorion ruptures during eclosion. The aquatic tadpoles then enter an endotrophic phase, subsisting entirely on residual yolk before the onset of exogenous feeding. Field surveys indicate that at a stable water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], the period from gamete fusion to the first feeding of the free-swimming larva spans approximately 60 days, a duration that aligns with the oxygen-dependent developmental rates characteristic of salamandrid amphibians in lentic habitats. The initial body length at hatching imposes constraints on the larval feeding ecology, as the buccal apparatus of these newly emerged tadpoles is adapted to capture only the smallest zooplankton prey available in their natal pools.

In contrast to their modest neonatal dimensions, adult female Southern banded newts attain a maximum snout–vent length of 4.8 centimeters [Li = 4.8 centimeters], a measurement derived from extensive museum specimen series and corroborated by field-based morphometric studies. This ultimate SVL for females is notably smaller than that of the related Triturus cristatus, reflecting differing allometric growth trajectories between the two genera. The corresponding asymptotic wet weight for females at this body size is approximately 1.8 grams [Wwi = approximately 1.8 grams], a value that was estimated through intraspecific scaling relationships calibrated on the larger-bodied crested newt. This relatively low adult mass suggests that female Ommatotriton vittatus allocate a significant proportion of their somatic resources toward oocyte production rather than continued skeletal growth following the completion of metamorphosis. The transition from the aquatic tadpole to the terrestrial juvenile stage occurs after a pronounced metamorphic climax involving tail resorption and skin keratinisation, and it is during this post-metamorphic phase that sexual size dimorphism begins to emerge.

Males of the species ultimately reach a slightly larger snout–vent length of 5.1 centimeters [Li = 5.1 centimeters], a sexually dimorphic difference that is commonly observed in urodeles where male–male competition for access to amplexing females is prevalent. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for males is 2.1 grams [Wwi = 2.1 grams], indicating that the greater skeletal length is accompanied by a proportional increase in somatic tissue mass relative to the female morph. This body mass advantage may confer benefits during the reproductive season, when males must actively patrol aquatic territories and engage in courtship displays. At the controlled laboratory temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], the lifespan of this species extends to 8 years [am = 8 years], a maximum longevity that is relatively lengthy for a salamandrid of this body size and that underscores a slow-paced life history strategy. Such an extended lifespan allows individuals to buffer against years of poor recruitment, a common feature of amphibian populations inhabiting unpredictable Mediterranean temporary water bodies.

The timing of sexual maturation in the Southern banded newt exhibits a clear sex-specific divergence, a pattern linked to the differing energetic demands of gametogenesis and reproductive behaviour. Under captive conditions maintained at 19 °C [T = 19 °C], females reach puberty at 4 years since birth [tp = 4 years since birth], a relatively protracted developmental period that likely reflects the time required to accumulate sufficient lipid stores for vitellogenesis. This age at puberty is considerably later than that observed in many other pond-breeding urodeles of equivalent adult size. Males, by contrast, attain sexual maturity more rapidly, with puberty occurring at 3 years since birth [tp = 3 years since birth] when reared at a constant 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. This earlier maturation in males is consistent with a life history strategy in which the earlier onset of reproductive activity provides a competitive advantage for securing breeding territories, even at a smaller body size than that ultimately achieved at asymptotic mass.

Reproductive output in this species is closely tied to the thermal regime of the breeding habitat. At a water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], gravid females deposit an average of 50 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 50 eggs per clutch], with most individuals producing a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This yields a maximum daily reproduction rate equivalent to approximately 0.14 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.14 eggs per day], reflecting a low daily output constrained by the energetic costs of oogenesis in a seasonal environment. This low fecundity per event is typical of species that produce large, yolk-rich ova, which in turn support the extended endotrophic larval phase observed immediately after eclosion. The annual reproductive cycle is synchronised with the onset of autumn rains, which fill temporary breeding pools and trigger the migration of reproductively active adults from their terrestrial refugia. During the brief aquatic breeding season, males engage in amplexus and external fertilisation of the egg mass, and the resulting larvae develop rapidly to complete metamorphosis before the ponds desiccate in the summer months.
